archetype.name: Pretender (pass rush and close games)
archetype.definition: A 7-2 team whose middle-of-the-pack efficiency says it is closer to a .500 club, kept on top of the AFC West by an elite pass rush, clean protection, a turnover edge and a perfect record in one-score games.

report.headline: A 7-2 record built on sacks, takeaways and close wins, not dominance
report.take:
Denver sits atop the AFC West at 7-2, but the underlying team is ordinary. Net EPA ranks 15th, the offense and defense both sit in the middle of the league, and a +12 point differential implies 4.7 wins, not seven. The 2.26 wins over expected lead the league, and the Broncos have won every one-score game they have played. That gap between record and play is the first thing to understand about this team.

What keeps them winning is a specific, real formula. The pass rush is among the league's best: 26 sacks (3rd) and a QB hit rate (2nd) that turns drives into punts and creates the takeaways (13, 5th) behind a turnover margin that ranks 5th. On the other side, Bo Nix plays behind a line that has allowed only 11 sacks, with a sack rate 3rd-best in the league. Look at the 17-14 win over Seattle: 107 passing yards, but five sacks and three takeaways. A good share of these wins came from the defense deciding drives, not from the offense moving the ball.

The numbers hide how little the offense produces between the 20s. Denver ranks 30th in yards per game and 28th in offensive success rate, and the run game manages 3.42 yards a carry (26th) behind a line that is good in pass protection but gives little before contact. The defense has its own leak. It ranks 25th in yards allowed, 26th in rush EPA allowed, 28th in explosive runs allowed and 31st in missed tackle rate, which is how Kansas City ran for 220 yards in the opener. History says some of this close-game knack is real under Sean Payton: the 2025 team went 14-3 with the league's best one-score record. It also says the defense has slid from 1st in EPA in 2024 to 8th last year to 13th now.

The trend is better than the season line. The passing game has posted positive EPA in each of the last three games after a rough first half. The schedule ahead is soft, with Miami, the Jets, the winless Chargers and two Raiders games still to come. Denver is likely to keep winning more than its efficiency deserves for a while yet, but a team that lives in one-score games will eventually lose some of them. The secondary injuries coming out of the bye matter more than they would for a team with a bigger margin.

strengths.title: A pass rush that wins games
strengths.body: Denver gets home as well as almost anyone, with 26 sacks and the league's second-best QB hit rate. The rush has finished drives in nearly every win, including five sacks each against the Chargers and Seattle. It is the most repeatable piece of the defense, though losing Uwazurike to injured reserve thins the rotation.

strengths.title: Nix is kept clean
strengths.body: The line allows a 3.5% sack rate (3rd) and the second-lowest QB hit rate, with only 11 sacks taken all year. That protection is why a low-efficiency offense rarely melts down into negative plays and turnovers. Seven giveaways in nine games is a ball-security profile that should hold.

strengths.title: Winning the turnover battle
strengths.body: A turnover margin ranked 5th has propped up a team that is outgained most weeks, and it ties directly to the pass rush forcing hurried throws. Takeaways swing more from year to year than sacks do, so expect this edge to shrink rather than disappear.

concerns.title: The record outruns the point differential
concerns.body: Seven wins against a differential worth 4.7 is the biggest overperformance in the league. It rests on a perfect one-score record that rarely survives a full season. The Broncos also did this in 2025, so Payton's clubs may close better than most, but the expected wins will drift back toward the real level of play. A 7-2 team with 15th-ranked net EPA has no cushion.

concerns.title: Soft run defense and poor tackling
concerns.body: The rush defense ranks 26th in EPA allowed and 28th in explosive runs allowed, and the 31st-ranked missed tackle rate explains a lot of it. A defense built to get after passers can be run at, as Kansas City showed in Week 1. It is a structural flaw, not a fluke, and with both starting safeties hurt the last line of defense is thinner.

concerns.title: An offense that struggles to sustain drives
concerns.body: Denver ranks 30th in yards per game and 28th in success rate. A run game averaging 3.42 yards a carry leaves Nix in obvious passing downs, and the team leans pass-heavy (6th in pass rate over expected). The recent passing uptick is real, but this unit depends on the defense and special teams shortening the field.

trend.note: Denver hasn't lost since early October. The passing game has turned from negative EPA in several early games to positive EPA in each of the last three (7.4 against Kansas City, 7.3 at Carolina), though most wins have still come by one score.

nextGame.headline: Rested Broncos host a Raiders defense that can't stop anything
nextGame.body:
Denver comes off a bye with 14 days of rest to host a 4-5 Raiders team whose defense ranks last in points and yards allowed. Las Vegas is 28th in pass EPA allowed, 31st in success rate allowed and dead last against short passes, which suits an offense that wins on timing throws more than chunk plays. The danger is that the Raiders score: their offense is 8th in points per game with a top-10 passing attack under Kirk Cousins, and their line allows sacks at the league's second-lowest rate, which blunts Denver's best weapon. The Raiders can't run at all (32nd in yards per carry), so Denver's leaky run defense may not get punished the way it usually could.

Availability favors Las Vegas more than the records suggest. Denver's two starting safeties, Talanoa Hufanga and Brandon Jones, are both out with return estimates of game day. Cornerback Kris Abrams-Draine is also out, and starting corner Riley Moss is questionable after a concussion, leaving a patched secondary to face Cousins. Jaylen Waddle, the team's leading target, is questionable with a concussion as well. The Raiders' report is light: rotational DT Thomas Booker IV and backup center Trey Zuhn III, both with return estimates before this game.

waysToWin.title: Live in the short passing game
waysToWin.body: Las Vegas allows the most EPA in the league on short throws and a top-two success rate allowed, so Nix can move the chains underneath without needing the deep ball. Receivers lined up as WR2 have feasted on this defense. That points to Courtland Sutton, or to whoever slides into that role if Waddle sits.

waysToWin.title: Finish drives in the red zone
waysToWin.body: The Raiders give up touchdowns on 71% of red-zone trips (28th), a rare chance for an offense that usually struggles to sustain drives to turn its trips into sevens. Converting there would give Denver a margin beyond its usual one score.

waysToWin.title: Make Las Vegas one-dimensional
waysToWin.body: The Raiders' run game ranks 30th in EPA and last in yards per carry, which hides Denver's weakest defensive unit. If Denver gets an early lead, Cousins has to throw into the league's third-best sack-producing rush on obvious passing downs.

waysToLose.title: Cousins picks apart a depleted secondary
waysToLose.body: With both starting safeties and a corner out, and Moss uncertain, Denver faces a top-10 passing offense with backups at the back. Denver is already 28th against tight ends by EPA per target, and that kind of weakness widens when the safeties are missing.

waysToLose.title: The Raiders' rush flips the turnover script
waysToLose.body: Las Vegas generates pressure at the league's third-highest rate and has 14 takeaways, one more than Denver. If the Raiders win the turnover battle, the Broncos lose their usual cushion, and an offense ranked 30th in yards has little room for error.

waysToLose.title: The pass rush gets neutralized
waysToLose.body: The Raiders allow sacks at the league's second-lowest rate, so Denver's game-wrecking rush may not get home often. Without sacks and short fields, this becomes a shootout against an offense that scores 26.4 a game, and Las Vegas' 7th-ranked special teams can tilt field position.

nextGame.watch: Whether Hufanga and Jones make it back from their game-day return estimates. If they don't, watch how Cousins attacks a secondary of backups.

restOfSeason.body:
The schedule is kind: Miami, the Jets and the winless Chargers all rank in the bottom third on at least one side of the ball, and Las Vegas appears twice. Only Pittsburgh and Buffalo look like true tests. That gives Denver a real path to the division and double-digit wins even as its luck evens out. The pass rush and the clean pocket should hold. The perfect one-score record and a turnover edge this large probably won't, so expect a loss or two in games the Broncos are currently winning.

The ceiling is capped by the offense. Unless the run game improves or the late-season passing gains stick, Denver stays a team that needs its defense to create short fields. That gets harder if the secondary injuries linger, and it will be tested by Buffalo's 3rd-ranked offense in Week 16. Kansas City sits a half-game back and is the main threat to the division lead.
swingFactors: Health of both starting safeties and Riley Moss
Whether the recent passing efficiency holds
Close-game and turnover luck evening out

confidence.note: Nine games with a stable QB, but heavy close-game variance and fresh secondary injuries.
